description:
Study in Germany for Free (2027): Tuition Fees, Living Costs & Funding

Direct answer box (first 50 words):

Germany remains one of the few study destinations where public universities charge no tuition for most programmes — but "free" means no tuition fees, not zero cost. Budget for semester contributions of roughly €150–€350 per semester, a blocked account of about €11,904 for the visa, and monthly living costs of €900–€1,300.

What "tuition-free" actually means in 2027

Public universities in Germany do not charge tuition for the vast majority of Bachelor's and consecutive Master's programmes — for international students too. Three things are often confused with tuition:

  1. Semester contribution (Semesterbeitrag): €150–€350 per semester, covering administration, student services and usually a regional transport ticket. Everyone pays it, including Germans.
  2. Non-consecutive Master's exceptions: some states (notably Baden-Württemberg) charge non-EU students €1,500 per semester for certain programmes. Check your specific course.
  3. Private universities: these do charge tuition (€10,000+ per year) and are a different market entirely.

The rule of thumb: find the course's fee page, not a general article — including this one. Fee rules are state-level and course-level, and they change.

One-off costs applicants forget

  • Blocked account: to get the student visa you must show roughly €11,904 (2026 rate, held in advance) — see our German blocked account guide for providers, alternatives and current amounts.
  • Deposit and first rent (often two to three months' rent up front)
  • Semester contribution on enrolment
  • Enrolment documents: translated and certified transcripts can cost €100–€300

Can you realistically fund yourself? Four routes

1. Scholarships

The DAAD is Germany's flagship funder — €992/month for Master's students and around €1,400/month for doctoral candidates on its main schemes — but dozens of political foundations (Friedrich Ebert, Konrad Adenauer, Heinrich Böll and others) fund international students too. Research-focused students can also start with a funded route like the Max Planck internship, which pays €1,300/month plus free housing for 12–14 weeks and often becomes a stepping stone into funded PhD positions.

2. Working alongside studies

International students may work 140 full days or 280 half days per year under current student visa rules. A typical HiWi (research assistant) or minijob pays €13–€17/hour, which realistically covers a meaningful part of living costs. Warning: students whose German is weak usually find English-sufficient jobs in bigger cities only.

3. PhD employment

At doctoral level, "free study" is the wrong frame: most German PhDs are paid jobs (TV-L E13, 50–75%) rather than self-funded study. If you aim for a doctorate, you may need no personal funding at all — see how German PhD pay works.

4. Family savings + part-time work

The classic route: blocked account for the visa, then part-time income plus careful budgeting in a small university town rather than Munich.

Step-by-step: getting to a German university for 2027

  1. Choose programmes, not just cities. Use the official DAAD database and check admission requirements per course — our guide to finding the right DAAD scheme covers scholarship matching.
  2. Check language requirements early. English-taught Master's usually need IELTS ~6.5; German-taught programmes need certified German (often TestDaF 4 / DSH-2). Our IELTS vs TOEFL vs PTE comparison helps you pick a test accepted broadly.
  3. Prepare documents — certified translations, APS certificate (for China, India, Vietnam), Uni-Assist evaluation where required. This stage alone takes 2–4 months; the 12-month application timeline keeps it on schedule.
  4. Apply via Uni-Assist or the university portal by the deadline — winter semester deadlines typically fall between January and July; summer intake is smaller.
  5. Secure funding evidence for the visa (blocked account, scholarship letter, or sponsor declaration).
  6. Apply for the student visa at the German embassy/consulate in your country — allow 6–12 weeks.
  7. Find housing before you fly — this is genuinely the hardest step. Studierenwerk halls waitlists are long in big cities; temporary accommodation + in-person searching is a normal strategy.

Is Germany still worth it compared to the UK?

For most self-funding students, yes: no tuition plus moderate living costs versus £20,000+ international tuition in the UK is a decisive gap. The trade-offs are longer degree structures, German-language daily life, and a housing market that punishes late starters. A full side-by-side is in our UK vs Germany vs Netherlands PhD comparison.

Frequently asked questions

Is university really free in Germany for international students? At most public universities for most programmes, yes — you pay only the semester contribution. Exceptions: Baden-Württemberg's non-EU fee for some programmes and all private universities.

How much money do I need in the bank for a German student visa? Around €11,904 (2026 blocked-account rate) for one year, adjusted annually. Alternatives include a scholarship award letter or a sponsor's declaration. Amounts change — verify with your embassy.

Can I study in Germany without IELTS? Some universities accept a Medium of Instruction certificate or prior English-taught degrees, but requirements are course-specific and tightening. See our guide to applying without IELTS.

What is the cheapest city to study in Germany? Smaller university towns (e.g. in Saxony, Thuringia or parts of NRW outside Cologne/Düsseldorf) typically offer rents 30–40% below Munich or Hamburg with the same tuition-free courses.

Official sources

Tuition rules, visa amounts and blocked-account figures come from German federal and state regulations and change annually. Confirm current figures on daad.de, your university's fee page and the German embassy before making financial decisions.
